meta.title: Doubled Participation
meta.skill_frame: Argument and evidence: two counts of different acts set side by side as growth.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.86, 6.00 and 6.05 on the three parts (104, 103 and 101 words), 5.94 together. The chart puts finishers beside signers, so the reader has to track which act each count measured before the difference can mean growth.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for argument_evidence 4.3, band 4.3, sequence 5. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A library page that compares children who finished a reading list with children who signed a card.
source.avoided: No library name, town, or program name.

session.difficulty_basis: Forty finishers are compared with eighty signers, so the doubling measures a wider net rather than more reading.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: A library prints a page about its summer reading program, and the page says participation doubled. It shows the change in a small chart with two bars and a line of text above them. Last summer, it reports, forty children finished the reading list of ten books. This summer eighty children took part. The chart draws a bar for each year in the same size box. Forty to eighty is a doubling, and the page says so twice in its first paragraph. The library asks the town for more money for next summer, and the chart is the reason it gives for the request.
passage.part_2: The two numbers do not count the same thing, and the page never says they do. Last summer's forty are children who finished a list of ten books and brought the list back to the desk. This summer's eighty are children who signed a card at the front desk. A card takes a moment at the desk and commits them to nothing. A child who signed a card and read nothing counts in the second number, and that child could never have counted in the first. The page puts a count of finishers beside a count of signers and calls the difference growth.
passage.part_3: Two numbers can be compared only when they measure the same act, and these two do not. Here one measures books read and the other measures a name on a card, and the chart sets them side by side without a note. The program may well have grown, and the library may deserve the money it asks for. But the chart compares a wide net with a narrow one. The clause that would explain the difference is missing from the page. A reader who wants to know whether more children read this summer needs the same count taken in both years.

items.prompt: What does the library's page claim?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. That participation in the summer program doubled.
help: The sentence about participation carries the claim.
It names the size of the change.
accept_ideas: participation doubled
twice as many children took part
the program doubled
twice the participation
not_required: how many books the library owns
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.ask: The page asks for money later. What does it claim about the program first?

items.prompt: A reader says the page shows twice as many children read this summer. Is that supported? Say why.

tutor_only.confirm: No. The two summers counted different acts, and a card is not the list.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The forty finished a list of ten books and the eighty signed a card, so the chart compares reading with signing.
tutor_only.tell: No. Signing a card is not finishing the list, so the chart compares two different acts.
help: The sentences about the forty and the eighty show the two acts.
They say what each count required.
tutor_only.core_idea: The two summers counted different acts: finishing the list against signing a card.
accept_ideas: no, a card is not the reading list
no, the page compares reading with signing
no, the two counts measure different things
no, signing up is not reading

if_they_say.when: the student says forty to eighty is a doubling, so the page is right
if_they_say.ask: A doubling of what? What did a child have to do to be counted each year?

tutor_only.full_idea: No, because the two summers counted different acts: finishing the list against signing a card.

items.prompt: What would the page need to show more children read this summer?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The same count, finishers, taken in both summers.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The page would need the number of children who finished the list in each summer, counted the same way both years.
tutor_only.tell: The number of finishers for both summers, counted the same way.
help: The sentences about the two acts name what has to match.
They show the count to repeat in both years.
